analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal sugar price supports and marketing quotas to bring sugar prices down.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan sugar-program phase-out with 74 cosponsors never left the House Agriculture subcommittee it was sent to in April 1997 and never got a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would gradually wind down the federal sugar program: loan rates for sugarcane would drop from 18¢ to 14¢ per pound between 1998 and 2002, the loans would stop being "nonrecourse" (meaning processors could no longer hand the sugar to the government instead of repaying), and all federal price support for the 2003 crop onward would end. It would also repeal sugar marketing quotas and allotments, which limit how much sugar can be sold in the US, and direct the President to keep adequate sugar flowing into the US market at no more than the higher of the world price or the falling loan rate.
analysis.who_benefits: American households, who pay well above the world price for sugar under the current program of guaranteed loans and marketing quotas, and taxpayers, who back the Commodity Credit Corporation loans that processors could walk away from. Sugar-using food manufacturers — candy, baked goods, cereals — would also see lower input costs. Prices would fall gradually: the bill keeps a floor at the higher of the world price or the declining loan rate through 2002, then eliminates support entirely.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the raw cane sugar loan rate from 18¢ to 14¢ per pound in steps between the 1998 and 2002 crops, and makes all loans recourse, ending the arrangement where a processor facing a price drop could forfeit its sugar to the government instead of repaying the loan.
Ends every form of federal sugar price support — loans, payments, purchases, or other operations — for the 2003 and later crops, so the government would no longer prop up the price of sugar at all.
Repeals the sugar marketing quota and allotment provisions, ending federal restrictions on how much sugar can be marketed domestically.

During the phase-out, directs the President to use all available authority to ensure adequate raw sugar supplies at prices no greater than the higher of the world price or the loan rate, keeping a ceiling on consumer prices while supports are wound down.

The mechanism behind the savings: under the existing program, nonrecourse loans plus supply quotas keep the US price well above the lower world price. Removing the supports and quotas would let domestic sugar prices fall toward world levels, saving money on groceries and cutting costs for candy and food makers. (Mechanism is general knowledge; the supports and quotas the bill removes are in the sources.)

analysis.who_pays: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors would lose guaranteed prices roughly double world levels, the right to forfeit sugar to the government instead of repaying loans, and the supply restrictions that protect them from competition. Because world sugar prices are themselves depressed by heavy foreign subsidies (general knowledge), some US growers — particularly smaller family sugar beet farms and the rural processing towns that depend on them — could not survive at world prices and would exit. Taxpayers would pay nothing; they would stop backing CCC sugar loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sugar cane and beet growers, processors

drawbacks.text: The bill removes all support by the 2003 crop, including marketing quotas that currently shelter domestic growers [S2][S3]. Because the world price is depressed by subsidized foreign production (general knowledge), growers who cannot compete at world prices — often smaller family sugar beet farms and the rural processing towns that depend on them — could go out of business, and US production could shift to countries that subsidize their own growers.

Consumer savings are back-loaded: the loan rate only reaches 14¢ per pound with the 2002 crop, and the recourse-loan conversion applies only after fiscal 1997, so prices stay near current levels for the first years of the phase-out.

The bill keeps a price floor at the higher of the world price or the loan rate through 2002, so if the world price spiked, US consumers would still pay above the loan-rate level during the transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers and taxpayers, the gains are large and long-lasting: ending a program that keeps sugar prices well above world levels lowers costs on every grocery shelf and removes taxpayer exposure to sugar loans. The real cost falls on a small, concentrated group of growers — and within that group, the burden would likely fall unevenly, hitting family sugar beet farms and one-industry rural towns hardest while the largest cane operations had the most to lose. An honest supporter would acknowledge the foreign-subsidy problem: if the US drops its supports while other countries keep theirs, some domestic production and the jobs tied to it may not survive. The bill tried to soften this with a five-year phase-in and a supply mandate during the transition, but it did nothing to address foreign subsidies after 2002.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee in April 1997, and it sat there — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Miller of Florida introduced the bill on April 17, 1997 with 57 original cosponsors named in the bill text.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day, and on April 28 was referred to the Subcommittee on Risk Management and Specialty Crops.
Cosponsorship grew to 74 members — 45 Republicans and 29 Democrats, including members from both parties from sugar-consuming districts.
No further action was ever taken: the subcommittee and full committee never held a markup or a vote, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar growers and processors came out ahead: by keeping the bill bottled up in committee, they preserved a program of guaranteed prices and marketing quotas that costs consumers and food manufacturers billions over the years it remains in place. Consumers kept paying above-world prices for sugar.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers and processors, who kept their program

for.name: Rep. Dan Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out sugar price supports and marketing quotas on April 17, 1997.

against.name: Rep. Bob Smith
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or floor action; it died in the Subcommittee on Risk Management and Specialty Crops. (His chairmanship and well-documented defense of the sugar program are general knowledge; the absence of any committee action is in the record.)

against.name: Sugar growers and processors (American Sugar Alliance)
against.role: Industry groups representing cane and beet growers
against.what_they_did: Opposed reform of the sugar program and defended the loan and quota system that the bill would have eliminated.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 45 Republicans and 29 Democrats — but the bill never reached a vote, so the chamber's actual partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
industries.note: The program this bill phases out guarantees growers prices well above world levels through nonrecourse government loans and marketing quotas, with benefits concentrated among a small number of large growers and processors. Ending it would cut their revenue and remove forfeitures and quotas; the industry's interest ran directly against consumers'.

Sugar is a major input for candy, baked goods, and cereal makers, and the program's above-world prices raise their costs. The bill would deliver cheaper sugar to them and to their customers; confectionery and food manufacturing jobs were a recurring argument in the sugar-policy debate.
